title: Architecture-dependent Effects of Trade-offs on Evolutionary Navigability and Epistasis
summary: The structure of the genotype-phenotype map plays a central role in determining how populations move through fitness landscapes, yet less is known about how this structure interacts with environmental constraints and fitness trade-offs. Here, we study evolution on a tunable multilayer genotype-phenotype map in which binary genotypes are transformed through successive feed-forward layers before being evaluated by phenotype-level fitness functions. We explicitly model the phenotype to fitness transformation in order to compare an emergent trade-off fitness with a no-trade-off control. We explore different map architecture as models of more and less complex genotype-phenotype relationships by tuning the genotype length and number of layers. We find that ruggedness and navigability have a complex, architecture-dependent relationship. Landscapes with few local maxima can still have low navigability for wide and shallow maps, and navigability is high even at mean values of ruggedness for wide and deep maps. Trade-offs increase navigability in wide and shallow maps, while their effect is muted in other architectures. The effect of trade-offs on epistasis depends on evolutionary history. While trade-offs change which mutational neighborhoods are sampled by evolution, the background degree of epistatic interactions is set by map architecture. Finally, we use our framework to investigate micro-evolution of high-fitness populations and show that temporal covariance in allele-frequency changes can arise from the internal structure of a rugged genotype-phenotype map, producing signatures that resemble short-term alternating selection.

AI.tldr: This paper studies evolution on tunable multilayer genotype-phenotype maps, finding that landscape ruggedness and navigability have complex, architecture-dependent relationships, and that trade-offs increase navigability in wide/shallow maps while having muted effects elsewhere. Trade-offs also alter which mutational neighborhoods are sampled, but background epistasis is set by map architecture. The framework further shows that temporal covariance in allele-frequency changes can arise from map structure alone, mimicking signatures of alternating selection.
AI.motivation: While the structure of the genotype-phenotype map is known to shape how populations traverse fitness landscapes, less is understood about how this structure interacts with environmental constraints and fitness trade-offs—prompting a systematic investigation into these interactions.
AI.method: The authors construct a tunable multilayer genotype-phenotype map where binary genotypes pass through successive feed-forward layers before phenotype-level fitness evaluation. They explicitly model phenotype-to-fitness transformations to compare an emergent trade-off fitness against a no-trade-off control, and vary genotype length and number of layers to model differently complex map architectures.
AI.result: Ruggedness and navigability show complex, architecture-dependent relationships: few local maxima can still yield low navigability in wide/shallow maps, while navigability remains high even at mean ruggedness in wide/deep maps. Trade-offs enhance navigability only in wide/shallow maps. Trade-off effects on epistasis are history-dependent, but background epistasis is architecture-determined. The framework also reveals that temporal covariance in allele-frequency changes can emerge from map structure, resembling short-term alternating selection.
AI.conclusion: Genotype-phenotype map architecture fundamentally shapes evolutionary dynamics in ways that are non-trivially coupled to fitness trade-offs, and internal map structure alone can produce evolutionary signatures that might otherwise be misattributed to fluctuating selection.

title: SurfSpec: Enhancing Off-Target-Agnostic Specificity by Bounding Pocket-Ligand Geometric Mismatch
summary: Lead optimization in structure-based drug design aims to improve target binding while avoiding unintended interactions with off-target pockets. However, existing affinity-driven methods do not explicitly control specificity, whereas current specificity-aware approaches commonly require prior knowledge of off-target structures. We address off-target-agnostic specificity-aware lead optimization by analyzing the geometric mismatch between a ligand and the target pocket. We provide a conservative specificity lower bound for geometrically separated off-targets without requiring access to off-target structures. By metricizing pocket--ligand mismatch, the triangle inequality shows that reducing target--ligand mismatch improves a conservative lower bound on mismatch to a separated off-target class, which can be translated into a specificity lower bound through an empirical geometry--affinity calibration. Motivated by this analysis, we introduce SurfSpec, an off-target-agnostic lead optimization framework that iteratively grows ligands toward under-occupied regions of the target pocket surface. SurfSpec alternates between linker generation toward selected target-surface patches, which provides geometric pseudo-labels, and refinement under a pocket-conditioned ligand prior, which restores these pseudo-labels into valid ligands. On the CrossDocked2020 test set, SurfSpec reduces geometric mismatch and outperforms evaluated off-target-agnostic lead optimization baselines in empirical specificity, while maintaining competitive target-affinity improvement.

AI.tldr: SurfSpec is an off-target-agnostic framework for specificity-aware lead optimization that grows ligands toward under-occupied regions of the target pocket surface, using geometric mismatch minimization guided by triangle-inequality-based theoretical guarantees.
AI.motivation: Existing affinity-driven lead optimization methods do not explicitly control specificity, while current specificity-aware approaches require prior knowledge of off-target structures, which is often unavailable. The authors aim to achieve specificity without needing off-target structural information.
AI.method: SurfSpec iteratively grows ligands toward under-occupied regions of the target pocket surface. It alternates between (1) linker generation toward selected target-surface patches providing geometric pseudo-labels, and (2) refinement under a pocket-conditioned ligand prior to restore pseudo-labels into valid ligands. The approach is theoretically motivated by conservative specificity lower bounds derived from the triangle inequality on pocket-ligand mismatch.
AI.result: On the CrossDocked2020 test set, SurfSpec reduces geometric mismatch, outperforms evaluated off-target-agnostic lead optimization baselines in empirical specificity, and maintains competitive target-affinity improvement.
AI.conclusion: Geometric mismatch analysis can enable specificity-aware lead optimization without off-target knowledge, providing both theoretical guarantees and practical performance improvements.

title: Sparse concept attribution for histomorphological hypothesis generation from whole-slide classifiers
summary: Histology images contain rich morphological information and can provide insights into pathological processes. However, deriving hypotheses relating morphological phenotypes to clinical attributes is bottlenecked by a manual image interpretation step. Here, we demonstrate that this process can be automated through interpretable deep learning. We present SCOPE, a method to interpret slide-level classifiers by combining pathology-specific vision--language models with sparse concept attribution onto a generalist histomorphological concept bank. To measure whether such explanations recover known morphology, we introduce MorphoRecoveryBench, a benchmark of seven tasks with pathologist-curated reference descriptions. On this benchmark, dense concept attribution is indistinguishable from a random baseline, whereas sparse attribution recovers substantial known morphology; decomposing the pooled slide embedding reaches similar explanation correctness at a fraction of the computational cost. Post-hoc interpretation of whole-slide classifiers can thus generate morphological hypotheses at scale, for expert validation.

AI.tldr: SCOPE automates morphological hypothesis generation from histology slides by combining vision-language models with sparse concept attribution onto a histomorphological concept bank. Using a new benchmark (MorphoRecoveryBench), they show sparse attribution recovers known morphology substantially better than dense attribution (which is near random), while a cheaper decomposition approach achieves similar correctness.
AI.motivation: Histology images contain rich morphological information relevant to pathological processes, but deriving hypotheses linking morphology to clinical attributes is bottlenecked by manual, time-consuming image interpretation by experts. Automating this process would enable hypothesis generation at scale for expert validation.
AI.method: SCOPE interprets slide-level classifiers by combining pathology-specific vision-language models with sparse concept attribution onto a generalist histomorphological concept bank. The authors introduce MorphoRecoveryBench, a benchmark of seven tasks with pathologist-curated reference descriptions, to evaluate whether explanations recover known morphology across dense attribution, sparse attribution, and a pooled slide embedding decomposition approach.
AI.result: On MorphoRecoveryBench, dense concept attribution performs no better than a random baseline, while sparse attribution recovers substantial known morphology. Decomposing the pooled slide embedding achieves similar explanation correctness at significantly lower computational cost.
AI.conclusion: Post-hoc interpretation of whole-slide classifiers can effectively generate morphological hypotheses at scale, offering a viable automated alternative to manual image interpretation—though sparse (rather than dense) attribution is crucial for meaningful recovery of known morphology.

title: Advances in Machine Learning for Directed Evolution: A Five-Year Retrospective
summary: The last five-plus years have seen many protein engineering disciplines transformed by advances in machine learning (ML), but the same cannot be said for directed evolution. Reflecting on a previously co-authored perspective, I discuss why I believe this to be the case, arguing that a disconnect between the goals of machine-learning-assisted directed evolution (MLDE) researchers--"identify an optimal protein"--and the goals of directed evolution more broadly--"identify a sufficient protein given time and resource constraints"--is a principal culprit. As an example, I highlight how nearly all current MLDE methods neglect to account for the cost of DNA synthesis, resulting in strategies that have limited practical applicability regardless of the underlying models' capabilities. I close by discussing recent works that are exceptions to this overarching trend, and emphasize that the last five years of efforts in ML-assisted protein engineering and the prescribed reframe of MLDE objectives need not be mutually exclusive.

AI.tldr: This perspective argues that the limited impact of machine learning on directed evolution stems from a fundamental disconnect: MLDE researchers aim to "identify an optimal protein" while directed evolution practitioners seek "a sufficient protein given time and resource constraints." The paper highlights how MLDE methods ignore practical costs like DNA synthesis, limiting real-world applicability, and discusses recent exceptions while suggesting the two goals need not be mutually exclusive.
AI.motivation: The author reflects on why machine learning has transformed many protein engineering disciplines over the past five years but has not similarly advanced directed evolution, attributing this to a mismatch between MLDE research objectives (finding optimal proteins) and the practical goals of directed evolution (finding sufficient proteins under real-world constraints).
AI.method: This is a perspective/opinion piece that reflects on a previously co-authored perspective, presenting an argument about the disconnect between MLDE researchers' goals and directed evolution practitioners' objectives, using the neglect of DNA synthesis costs as a concrete example, and discussing recent exceptions to the prevailing trend.
AI.result: The paper identifies that most current MLDE methods fail to account for practical costs (like DNA synthesis), making them impractical regardless of model capability, while noting recent works that are exceptions and arguing that optimizing for "sufficient" rather than "optimal" proteins within resource constraints should be the reframed objective.
AI.conclusion: The author concludes that the five years of ML-assisted protein engineering efforts and the proposed reframing of MLDE objectives toward resource-aware, sufficiency-based goals need not be mutually exclusive, suggesting a path forward that integrates practical constraints into ML-driven protein engineering.

title: Enhancer-promoter proximity predicts transcriptional competence but not transcriptional output in the Drosophila brain
summary: How 3D genome architecture contributes to transcriptional specificity across neuronal cell types remains unclear. Here, we used multiplexed chromatin tracing to map chromatin architecture and cell identity at single-cell resolution in the adult Drosophila brain. We found that enhancer-promoter (E-P) proximity was increased in transcriptionally active compared with inactive neurons. Analysis of single traces revealed the existence of distinct proximal and distal E-P states, with active neurons enriched in the proximal state. However, this relationship broke down across active neuronal subtypes, where neither E-P proximity nor chromatin accessibility predicted transcriptional output. Thus, 3D genome organization distinguishes transcriptionally competent from inactive neuronal states without quantitatively specifying transcriptional output. Our findings support a model in which E-P proximity establishes a permissive structural state, while additional cell-type-specific regulatory mechanisms tune transcriptional output.

AI.tldr: This study uses multiplexed chromatin tracing in the adult Drosophila brain to map 3D genome architecture and cell identity at single-cell resolution, revealing that enhancer-promoter (E-P) proximity is increased in transcriptionally active neurons but does not quantitatively predict transcriptional output across active neuronal subtypes, supporting a model where E-P proximity establishes a permissive structural state rather than determining transcription.
AI.motivation: To understand how 3D genome architecture contributes to transcriptional specificity across different neuronal cell types, a question that remains poorly understood.
AI.method: Multiplexed chromatin tracing to map chromatin architecture and cell identity simultaneously at single-cell resolution in the adult Drosophila brain, analyzing E-P proximity states across neuronal subtypes.
AI.result: E-P proximity was higher in transcriptionally active neurons versus inactive ones, with distinct proximal and distal E-P states observed; however, across active neuronal subtypes, neither E-P proximity nor chromatin accessibility predicted transcriptional output.
AI.conclusion: 3D genome organization distinguishes transcriptionally competent neurons from inactive ones without quantitatively specifying transcriptional output, supporting a model where E-P proximity creates a permissive structural state, while other cell-type-specific regulatory mechanisms fine-tune transcription.

title: An Integrative Computational Approach to Predict Viral Epitopes by Targeting the MHC-TCR Complexation
summary: T-cell immunity acts as a major defense system against controlling viral infections in vertebrates. During viral entry, innate immune cells degrade the viral proteins (antigens) and present them on their surface via Major Histocompatibility (MHC) proteins. T-cell receptors (TCRs) recognize these antigens/peptides presented by MHC (pMHC), initiating a T-cell mediated immune response. Despite its significance, the mechanism by which pMHC-TCR binding triggers T-cell activation remains unclear. In this study, we employed an integrative computational approach combining Bioinformatics, Molecular Dynamics (MD) simulations, and Machine Learning (ML) to identify viral epitopes as potential vaccine candidates. We performed large-scale all-atom and coarse-grained MD simulations on MHC-peptide-TCR complexes embedded into dendritic and T-cells, for which experimental immunogenicity data is available. One hundred fifty such systems are simulated for 1 μs each to capture the conformational and dynamical changes that underlie T-cell activation. Our ML model (DynamiT), trained on simulation-derived structural and dynamical features extracted from 2500 time points, revealed key determinants responsible for T-cell activation with an accuracy of 73.3%. Notably, we have identified the bending of the TCR transmembrane region, major dynamic motions of the TCRα constant region and the buried surface area at the pMHC and TCR interface as critical factors influencing immune response initiation. Our approach unravels the mechanism of T-cell mediated immune response and helps ML-guided screening of viral epitopes for vaccine development.

AI.tldr: The authors used an integrative computational pipeline combining bioinformatics, MD simulations (all-atom and coarse-grained), and machine learning to study 150 MHC-peptide-TCR complexes embedded in cellular membranes. They trained an ML model (DynamiT) on simulation-derived features achieving 73.3% accuracy in predicting T-cell activation, identifying TCR transmembrane bending, TCRα constant region dynamics, and pMHC-TCR buried surface area as key determinants.
AI.motivation: Understanding how pMHC-TCR binding triggers T-cell activation is critical for vaccine development, yet the molecular mechanism remains unclear. The authors aim to computationally uncover the structural and dynamical determinants of T-cell activation.
AI.method: An integrative computational approach combining bioinformatics, large-scale all-atom and coarse-grained MD simulations (150 systems, 1 μs each) of MHC-peptide-TCR complexes embedded in dendritic and T-cell membranes, followed by machine learning (DynamiT) trained on structural and dynamical features from 2500 time points to classify T-cell activation.
AI.result: The ML model achieved 73.3% accuracy in predicting T-cell activation. Key determinants identified include TCR transmembrane region bending, major dynamic motions of the TCRα constant region, and buried surface area at the pMHC-TCR interface.
AI.conclusion: This work unravels the mechanistic basis of T-cell mediated immune response and provides an ML-guided platform for screening viral epitopes as vaccine candidates.

title: Coarse-Graining Agent-Based Models of Bacterial Infections
summary: Agent-based models (ABMs) provide a natural framework for representing cell-level rules and spatial heterogeneity in bacterial infections, but their computational cost limits their use for macroscopic tissue-scale simulations and broad parameter exploration. We derive a deterministic coarse-grained description for a class of bacterial-infection ABMs in which immune cells and extracellular bacteria diffuse, immune cells ingest nearby bacteria, and intracellular bacterial loads evolve through prescribed birth and clearance processes. The first coarse-grained model is a semidiscrete reaction--diffusion system that retains a discrete internal state for each immune-cell bacterial load while representing cell and bacterial populations by continuum concentration fields. The key technical step is the derivation of state-dependent effective ingestion rates from the microscopic ABM parameters: these rates are obtained by solving an auxiliary diffusion problem around a single bacterium and computing the flux of immune cells into the interaction region. We then take a continuum limit in the internal state variable, yielding a state-structured reaction--diffusion system in which intracellular dynamics appear as advection and diffusion in state space. Numerical comparisons with ensemble-averaged ABM simulations show close agreement in biologically motivated parameter regimes. The resulting framework preserves the rule-based structure of the ABM while producing PDE models that are substantially more tractable for large-scale simulation and parameter studies.

AI.tldr: This paper derives deterministic coarse-grained models (semidiscrete and fully continuum reaction-diffusion systems) from a class of agent-based models for bacterial infections, where effective ingestion rates are computed from microscopic parameters via auxiliary diffusion problems, enabling tractable large-scale PDE simulations that closely match ensemble-averaged ABM results.
AI.motivation: Agent-based models (ABMs) naturally capture cell-level rules and spatial heterogeneity in bacterial infections, but their computational cost severely limits their use for macroscopic tissue-scale simulations and broad parameter exploration, motivating the need for more tractable deterministic descriptions.
AI.method: The authors (1) construct a semidiscrete reaction-diffusion system retaining discrete internal states for immune-cell bacterial loads while representing cell/bacterial populations as continuum fields; (2) derive state-dependent effective ingestion rates by solving an auxiliary diffusion problem around a single bacterium and computing the immune-cell flux into the interaction region; (3) take a continuum limit in the internal state variable to obtain a state-structured reaction-diffusion system where intracellular dynamics manifest as advection and diffusion in state space.
AI.result: Numerical comparisons with ensemble-averaged ABM simulations demonstrate close agreement across biologically motivated parameter regimes, confirming that the coarse-grained PDE framework faithfully reproduces ABM behavior while being substantially more computationally tractable.
AI.conclusion: The derived framework preserves the rule-based structure of the ABM while producing PDE models that are significantly more scalable for large-scale simulation and parameter studies, bridging the gap between mechanistic cell-level modeling and macroscopic tissue-scale applications.

title: Structural control over equilibrium silicon and oxygen isotopic fractionation: A first-principles density-functional theory study
summary: Isotopic fractionation factors for oxygen and silicon in selected silicates (quartz, enstatite, forsterite, lizardite, kaolinite) have been calculated using first-principles methods. Good agreement between theory and experiment is obtained in the case of oxygen. In the case of silicon, agreement and differences with existing estimates of equilibrium fractionation factors are discussed. The relationships between silicon fractionation factors and oxygen fractionation factors, silicate polymerization degree and chemical composition is studied. The previously stated relationship with the polymerization degree of the mineral is not confirmed. Nevertheless, our calculation suggests that silicon fractionation depends on the cationic content of the mineral, in a way similar to oxygen.  Oxygen fractionation properties could thus provide some insights on silicon fractionation behavior.

AI.tldr: First-principles calculations of oxygen and silicon isotopic fractionation factors in five silicates (quartz, enstatite, forsterite, lizardite, kaolinite) show good agreement with experiment for oxygen, while silicon fractionation is found to depend on cationic content rather than polymerization degree, similar to oxygen.
AI.motivation: To accurately determine equilibrium isotopic fractionation factors for oxygen and silicon in silicate minerals and to understand the controlling factors behind silicon isotope fractionation, particularly testing whether polymerization degree or chemical composition governs the behavior.
AI.method: First-principles quantum mechanical calculations are used to compute isotopic reduced partition function ratios (β-factors) for oxygen and silicon in selected silicates, which are then compared with experimental estimates and analyzed for correlations with mineral structure and composition.
AI.result: Oxygen fractionation factors agree well with experiment. For silicon, the previously proposed relationship with the degree of polymerization is not confirmed; instead, silicon fractionation appears to depend on the cationic content of the mineral, analogous to oxygen behavior.
AI.conclusion: The study demonstrates that first-principles methods can reliably predict oxygen isotopic fractionation, and suggests that oxygen fractionation properties may serve as a proxy for predicting silicon isotopic fractionation behavior in silicates.

title: The Identification of Biological Stains at Crime Scenes: A Promising Role for Proteomics and Machine Learning
summary: Forensic body fluid identification is crucial for reconstructing crime scene events. While DNA analysis provides individualization, it lacks information about the fluid's origin. We developed and evaluated three complementary proteomic approaches using LC-HRMS/MS to identify blood, saliva, semen, urine, and vaginal fluid, including complex mixtures. The first method utilized fluid-specific peptide biomarkers, achieving high accuracy for pure fluids. The second employed peptide abundance ratios, demonstrating effectiveness in body fluid mixtures. The third, a machine learning model using Classifier Chain Random Forest, achieved 100% accuracy for pure fluids and promising results for mixtures. Our results revealed the complementarity of different tests, with the peptide-specific biomarker and machine-learning approaches being the most robust. This study demonstrates the potential of proteomics for comprehensive body fluid identification, offering valuable tools for forensic investigations.

AI.tldr: This study develops and evaluates three complementary proteomic approaches using LC-HRMS/MS for forensic body fluid identification (blood, saliva, semen, urine, vaginal fluid), including complex mixtures. The methods—peptide-specific biomarkers, peptide abundance ratios, and a Classifier Chain Random Forest machine learning model—demonstrate high accuracy for pure fluids and promising results for mixtures, with the biomarker and ML approaches proving most robust.
AI.motivation: Forensic body fluid identification is essential for crime scene reconstruction, but while DNA analysis can individualize samples, it cannot determine the origin of the fluid. There is a need for reliable methods to identify the source of body fluids, including when they are present in complex mixtures.
AI.method: Three complementary proteomic approaches using LC-HRMS/MS were developed and evaluated: (1) fluid-specific peptide biomarker identification for pure fluids, (2) peptide abundance ratio analysis for body fluid mixtures, and (3) a machine learning model employing Classifier Chain Random Forest.
AI.result: The peptide-specific biomarker method achieved high accuracy for pure fluids. The peptide abundance ratio approach demonstrated effectiveness in body fluid mixtures. The machine learning model achieved 100% accuracy for pure fluids and promising results for mixtures. The peptide-specific biomarker and machine-learning approaches were found to be the most robust.
AI.conclusion: The study demonstrates that proteomics offers comprehensive body fluid identification capabilities, providing valuable complementary tools for forensic investigations beyond what DNA analysis alone can offer.

title: Modeling Tissue Detachment and Rupture Using an Extended Vertex Model with T2-inverse Transitions
summary: The vertex model is widely used to describe the mechanics of epithelial tissues, but its conventional formulation assumes that all cells remain tightly packed and always share edges with their neighbors, making it difficult to represent local detachment or gap formation. Here, we propose a minimal extension of the vertex model that enables cell detachment by introducing a new topological transformation, T2-inverse, which acts as the inverse of the classical T2 transition. When the imbalance of forces acting on a vertex, quantified by a tension metric $T$, exceeds a threshold, the T2-inverse splits the vertex into multiple vertices and creates a closed polygon that is incorporated as a pseudo-cell. This operation allows the model to represent the emergence and propagation of local detachment events. Using this framework, we simulate the stretching of a cell sheet and show that force-induced local detachments can accumulate to produce macroscopic tissue rupture. These results demonstrate that the proposed model extends the capability of the vertex model to describe tissue-level breakdown processes, including detachment and tearing, and provides a foundation for studying a broader class of epithelial mechanical phenomena.

AI.tldr: The authors propose a minimal extension of the vertex model for epithelial tissues by introducing a new topological transformation called T2-inverse, which enables cell detachment and gap formation. When a tension metric exceeds a threshold, the transformation splits vertices and creates pseudo-cells, allowing simulation of tissue rupture under stretching.
AI.motivation: The conventional vertex model assumes cells remain tightly packed and share edges with neighbors, making it impossible to represent local detachment or gap formation in epithelial tissues.
AI.method: Introduces a T2-inverse topological transformation (inverse of the classical T2 transition) that splits a vertex into multiple vertices and creates a closed polygon incorporated as a pseudo-cell when a tension metric T exceeds a threshold.
AI.result: Simulations of cell sheet stretching show that force-induced local detachments can accumulate, leading to macroscopic tissue rupture.
AI.conclusion: The proposed model extends the vertex model's capability to describe tissue-level breakdown processes including detachment and tearing, providing a foundation for studying a broader class of epithelial mechanical phenomena.

title: High-Order Triadic Functional Connectivity in the Brain and Beyond
summary: Here, we report high-order functional network connectivity as a promising way for studying the brain connectome. Traditional functional connectivity approaches capture only pairwise relationships between brain regions, overlooking complex multivariate dependencies that underlie cognition and behavior. First, we demonstrated that high-order interactions capture more information and can distinguish between resting-state and task-state brain activity. Second, we introduce a matrix-based entropy-functional method for estimating triadic interactions, which are statistical dependencies among triplets of brain regions, and apply it to large-scale functional brain networks. The resulting triadic networks revealed distinct community patterns that complement those observed in traditional pairwise functional connectivity analyses and simultaneously capture additional connection information. Despite the potential combinatorial explosion of triadic configurations, the networks exhibited constrained and hierarchical structures that allowed computation and interpretation. These findings position triadic connectivity as a promising next-step functional connectivity framework for probing brain network organization and high-order neural interactions, while also highlighting key biological and technical challenges that require careful consideration.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes high-order functional network connectivity, specifically triadic interactions (statistical dependencies among triplets of brain regions), as a novel framework for studying the brain connectome. Using a matrix-based entropy-functional method, the authors estimate triadic interactions in large-scale functional brain networks, showing that high-order interactions capture more information than traditional pairwise approaches and can distinguish resting-state from task-state activity. The resulting triadic networks reveal distinct community patterns complementary to pairwise analyses, exhibiting constrained and hierarchical structures despite potential combinatorial explosion.
AI.motivation: Traditional functional connectivity approaches only capture pairwise relationships between brain regions, overlooking complex multivariate dependencies that underlie cognition and behavior. High-order interactions are proposed as a more informative way to study brain network organization.
AI.method: The authors introduce a matrix-based entropy-functional method for estimating triadic interactions—statistical dependencies among triplets of brain regions—and apply it to large-scale functional brain networks derived from resting-state and task-state data.
AI.result: High-order interactions capture more information and distinguish between resting-state and task-state brain activity. The resulting triadic networks reveal distinct community patterns that complement traditional pairwise functional connectivity analyses and simultaneously capture additional connection information. Despite potential combinatorial explosion of triadic configurations, the networks exhibit constrained and hierarchical structures enabling computation and interpretation.
AI.conclusion: Triadic connectivity is positioned as a promising next-step functional connectivity framework for probing brain network organization and high-order neural interactions, while also highlighting key biological and technical challenges that require careful consideration.

title: Axonal delay dispersion decides whether a neuron detects an event or a sequence, and predicts cortical column diameter
comment: 30 pages, 4 figures, under preparation for PLOS Computational Biology
summary: Cortical neurons fire sparsely -- often fewer than one spike per sensory window -- making rate coding insufficient and temporal coding a necessity. That conduction delays convert firing order into synchrony is long established. What governs which class of temporal feature a neuron detects -- one volley of coincident input, or two in a particular order -- has not been examined. We propose a delay-signature framework in which the axonal conduction delays converging on a dendritic branch constitute a physical key: only input sequences whose spike-time differences the delays compensate arrive synchronously, and coincidence detection, via calcium plateau thresholds, converts that synchrony into an all-or-none output. In simulations of an integrator-neuron model we report three results. First, a single physical scalar -- the dispersion of the delay set -- moves a population from event detection to order-selective sequence detection. The transition is emergent under random delays and connectivity: at narrow dispersion sequence detectors do not exist, and the dispersion at which they overtake event detectors tracks the inter-event interval with a slope statistically indistinguishable from one. This maps a computational distinction onto the anatomical one between myelinated and unmyelinated projections, making myelination a switch on what a neuron computes, not only a regulator of speed. Second, the same dispersion sets the code's limits: it bounds the longest codable interval and fixes an absolute timing tolerance of about a millisecond, with slowing better tolerated than speeding. Third, that millisecond window and horizontal conduction velocity together predict cortical column diameter, and the two areas with direct measurements fall where the relation puts them. One anatomically measurable parameter thus sets what a neuron detects and the limits of what it can represent.

AI.tldr: A delay-signature framework shows that axonal conduction delay dispersion on dendritic branches determines whether neurons act as event detectors or order-selective sequence detectors, with the narrowness of delay dispersion acting as a computational switch tied to myelination status.
AI.motivation: Cortical neurons fire sparsely, making temporal coding necessary rather than rate coding. While it is known that conduction delays convert firing order into synchrony, what determines which class of temporal feature a neuron detects (single coincidence volley vs. ordered pairs) has not been examined.
AI.method: Proposes a delay-signature framework where axonal conduction delays converging on a dendritic branch form a physical key: input sequences with spike-time differences compensated by delays arrive synchronously, and coincidence detection via calcium plateau thresholds converts that synchrony into all-or-none output. Simulations of an integrator-neuron model examine the effect of delay-set dispersion.
AI.result: Three results: (1) Dispersion of the delay set is a single scalar that moves a population from event detection to order-selective sequence detection, with the transition emergent under random delays and the transition dispersion tracking inter-event interval with slope of one, mapping onto the myelinated/unmyelinated anatomical distinction. (2) Same dispersion bounds the longest codable interval and fixes absolute timing tolerance (~1ms), with slowing better tolerated than speeding. (3) The millisecond window and horizontal conduction velocity predict cortical column diameter, matching the two areas with direct measurements.
AI.conclusion: A single anatomically measurable parameter (delay dispersion) sets both what a neuron detects (event vs. ordered sequence) and limits of what it can represent, linking computation to myelination and anatomy.

title: Enumerating Chemical Structures, Stereoisomers, and Stereogenic Units with Analytic Combinatorics
comment: Submitted to J. Math. Chem. 27 pages, 7 figures
summary: The enumeration of chemical structures traditionally relies on graph- and group-theoretic techniques, including Pólya theory, in order to account for stereochemical symmetries. These methods require bespoke derivations and methods for each molecular family of interest, and quickly become very intricate for nontrivial classes. In this work, we demonstrate that analytic combinatorics provides a unifying, highly extensible, and relatively simple framework for enumeration problems. Using the symbolic method, we show that classical counting problems, such as the enumeration of acyclic alkanes and other hydrocarbon families, can be naturally solved via concise combinatorial specifications of the class of interest. We first demonstrate the simplicity of this approach by replicating existing results in this framework, requiring significantly less work than previously necessary, and then extend these ideas to more complex problems, counting broader classes of molecules accounting for both tetrahedral and E/Z stereoisomerism, counting the distribution of stereogenic units, and enumerating achiral and meso compounds. All results are made reproducible through CombOL, our open-source software package which automates the translation of combinatorial specifications into generating functions using the symbolic method, and performs both univariate and multivariate enumeration.

AI.tldr: The paper presents analytic combinatorics as a unifying framework for enumerating chemical structures, replacing traditional graph/group-theoretic methods (e.g., Pólya theory). Using the symbolic method, the authors solve classical problems like acyclic alkane enumeration more simply, and extend to complex cases including tetrahedral and E/Z stereoisomerism, stereogenic unit distributions, and achiral/meso compounds—all made reproducible via their open-source software CombOL.
AI.motivation: Traditional enumeration of chemical structures relies on graph- and group-theoretic techniques like Pólya theory, which require bespoke derivations for each molecular family and become highly intricate for nontrivial classes. A simpler, more unifying and extensible framework is needed.
AI.method: The authors apply analytic combinatorics via the symbolic method, translating concise combinatorial specifications of molecular classes into generating functions. This framework is used to replicate classical results (e.g., acyclic alkanes) and extended to more complex problems involving stereoisomerism, stereogenic unit distributions, and achiral/meso compounds. Results are automated through CombOL, an open-source software package that translates specifications into generating functions for univariate and multivariate enumeration.
AI.result: The paper demonstrates that analytic combinatorics reproduces classical enumeration results (e.g., acyclic alkanes and hydrocarbons) with significantly less effort than traditional methods, and successfully extends to challenging problems including tetrahedral and E/Z stereoisomerism, stereogenic unit counting, and achiral/meso compound enumeration. CombOL makes all results reproducible.
AI.conclusion: Analytic combinatorics offers a unifying, highly extensible, and relatively simple framework for chemical enumeration problems, providing a strong modern alternative to classical group-theoretic approaches. The approach enables tractable solutions for complex stereochemical enumeration challenges previously requiring laborious bespoke derivations.

title: Tensor-based Brain Surface Modeling and Analysis
summary: We present a unified computational approach to tensor-based morphometry in detecting the brain surface shape differences between two clinical groups based on magnetic resonance images. Our approach is novel in a sense that we combined surface modeling, surface data smoothing and statistical analysis in a coherent unified mathematical framework. The cerebral cortex has the topology of a 2D highly convoluted sheet. Between two different clinical groups, the local surface area and curvature of the cortex may differ. It is highly likely that such surface shape differences are not uniform over the whole cortex. By computing how such surface metrics differ, the regions of the most rapid structural differences can be localized. To increase the signal to noise ratio, diffusion smoothing based on the explicit estimation of Laplace-Beltrami operator has been developed and applied to the surface metrics. As an illustration, we demonstrate how this new tensor-based surface morphometry can be applied in localizing the cortical regions of the gray matter tissue growth and loss in the brain images longitudinally collected in the group of children.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a unified computational framework for tensor-based morphometry that combines surface modeling, diffusion smoothing via Laplace-Beltrami operator estimation, and statistical analysis to detect and localize cortical surface shape differences between clinical groups in MRI data.
AI.motivation: The cerebral cortex is a highly convoluted 2D sheet whose local surface area and curvature may differ between clinical groups. These shape differences are likely non-uniform across the cortex, so a method is needed to localize regions of most rapid structural differences. Existing approaches treat surface modeling, smoothing, and statistics as separate steps rather than in a unified framework.
AI.method: The approach unifies surface modeling, surface data smoothing, and statistical analysis in a single coherent mathematical framework. It computes surface metric differences (local surface area and curvature) to localize structural differences. To improve signal-to-noise ratio, diffusion smoothing is applied to the surface metrics using explicit estimation of the Laplace-Beltrami operator.
AI.result: The method is demonstrated by localizing cortical regions of gray matter tissue growth and loss in longitudinal brain images collected from a group of children.
AI.conclusion: A unified tensor-based surface morphometry framework can effectively localize cortical structural differences between clinical groups, with potential applications in studying brain development and disease-related morphological changes.

title: Large-Language Models as a Cognitive Virus
summary: Large-language models (LLMs) are rapidly becoming part of human culture, reshaping how information is produced, transmitted, and used. Here we propose that their diffusion can be understood through a viral analogy, with LLM use spreading through populations, becoming embedded in cognitive and cultural practices. We model transitions among uncoupled, coupled, and persistently dependent users, and show that the interplay between social transmission, recovery, and collective reinforcement can generate tipping points and technological lock-in. A central consequence is the possibility of runaway dynamics: once a critical threshold is crossed, small increases in adoption can trigger rapid population-level shifts toward persistent dependence, with abrupt losses in cognitive competence. The same framework, however, identifies conditions for cognitive immunization, based on reducing transmission and facilitating reversibility. Our results highlight how LLM adoption may involve nonlinear collective transitions with important consequences for cognitive autonomy.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes understanding LLM adoption through a viral/epidemiological analogy, modeling transitions among uncoupled, coupled, and persistently dependent users to show that social transmission dynamics can generate tipping points, technological lock-in, and abrupt population-level shifts toward persistent dependence with cognitive competence loss.
AI.motivation: LLMs are becoming deeply embedded in human culture and cognitive practices, yet little is understood about the population-level dynamics of their adoption and how dependence on these tools might spread and become entrenched.
AI.method: The authors model transitions among three user states (uncoupled, coupled, and persistently dependent), examining the interplay between social transmission, recovery, and collective reinforcement within a viral-analogy framework.
AI.result: The framework reveals tipping points and technological lock-in: once a critical threshold is crossed, small adoption increases trigger rapid population-level shifts toward persistent dependence with abrupt cognitive competence losses. It also identifies conditions for "cognitive immunization" via reduced transmission and increased reversibility.
AI.conclusion: LLM adoption may involve nonlinear collective transitions with significant consequences for cognitive autonomy, highlighting the need to understand and potentially mitigate runaway dependence dynamics.

title: SimpleDesign: A Joint Model for Protein Sequence and Structure Codesign
comment: Published in Transactions on Machine Learning Research (TMLR), 2026. https://openreview.net/forum?id=wPfw7GkMns
summary: Proteins are fundamental to biological processes, with their function determined by the complex interplay between the amino acid sequence and the three-dimensional structure. Developing generative models capable of understanding this intrinsically multi-modal relationship is crucial for fields like drug discovery and protein engineering. Existing models often rely on a multi-stage training process where autoencoders that tokenize data into latent representations are trained in a first stage. Secondly, a generative model is trained on the latent representation of the autoencoder(s), i.e., generative modeling in a latent space. We hypothesize that this multi-stage training is not necessary to obtain performant co-design models and thus present SimpleDesign, an effective multi-modal protein design model trained directly in the data space. SimpleDesign leverages a single-stage end-to-end objective that combines discrete cross-entropy for sequences and a regression objective for structures. In order to effectively model the difference in sequence and structure modalities, we develop a Mixture-of-Transformer architecture that allows modality-specific processing while keeping global self-attention over both modalities. We train SimpleDesign on over 2M sequence-structure pairs achieving strong performance across co-design and unconditional sequence/structure generation benchmarks.

AI.tldr: SimpleDesign is an end-to-end multi-modal protein design model that generates sequences and structures jointly in a single training stage, using a Mixture-of-Transformer architecture to handle modality-specific processing while maintaining global self-attention over both modalities.
AI.motivation: Existing protein co-design models rely on multi-stage training, where autoencoders first tokenize data into latent representations and then a generative model is trained on those representations. The authors hypothesize this multi-stage approach is unnecessary for building performant co-design models.
AI.method: SimpleDesign uses a single-stage end-to-end objective combining discrete cross-entropy loss for sequences and a regression objective for structures. A Mixture-of-Transformer architecture enables modality-specific processing while preserving global self-attention across both sequence and structure modalities. The model is trained on over 2 million sequence-structure pairs directly in data space.
AI.result: SimpleDesign achieves strong performance on co-design benchmarks, as well as unconditional sequence and structure generation benchmarks, demonstrating that multi-stage latent-space training is not required for effective multi-modal protein design.
AI.conclusion: Direct data-space training with an appropriate architecture can match or exceed the performance of multi-stage latent-space approaches for multi-modal protein design, simplifying the training pipeline.

title: Neural-Network Maxent: a general extension with learned nonlinearity, applied to time-series for Desert Locust distribution modelling
summary: Species Distribution Modelling (SDM) is essential for understanding how environmental conditions shape biodiversity, particularly for destructive pests such as the Desert Locust (Schistocerca gregaria), whose breeding dynamics are tightly coupled to rapidly evolving environmental conditions. Maxent has become the dominant method for presence-only data, but its reliance on a linear combination of hand chosen feature transforms limits its ability to capture the nonlinear, temporal relationships common in ecological monitoring, where covariates such as precipitation, soil moisture, and vegetation indices evolve meaningfully over time. Standard implementations flatten time-series covariates into independent features, discarding sequential structure that carries critical signal. We introduce RNN Maxent, an extension of the Maxent framework that replaces the fixed feature dictionary with a neural network, specifically a Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU), trained end to end via backpropagation. The approach preserves Maxent's presence only statistical foundations, background normalization, and probability calibration, differing only in that the nonlinearity is learned from data rather than fixed in advance. We apply RNN Maxent to map suitable habitat for the Desert Locust using 50 day environmental time series derived from ERA5 Land, MODIS, and Sentinel 3, maintaining a 7 day gap between covariates and presence records to yield forecasting behavior. Compared against standard Maxent, RNN Maxent improves performance across metrics (ROC AUC 0.862 std 0.036 vs. 0.792; F1 0.671 std 0.056 vs. 0.590).

AI.tldr: The paper introduces RNN Maxent, an extension of the Maxent presence-only SDM framework that replaces fixed feature dictionaries with a Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU) trained end-to-end via backpropagation. Applied to Desert Locust habitat mapping using 50-day environmental time series, it preserves Maxent's statistical foundations while learning nonlinear temporal relationships, outperforming standard Maxent (ROC AUC 0.862 vs 0.792; F1 0.671 vs 0.590).
AI.motivation: Standard Maxent relies on linear combinations of hand-chosen feature transforms, which cannot capture nonlinear and temporal relationships in ecological data where covariates like precipitation, soil moisture, and vegetation evolve over time. Flattening time-series covariates into independent features discards critical sequential structure.
AI.method: Replace Maxent's fixed feature dictionary with a GRU neural network trained end-to-end via backpropagation. The approach maintains Maxent's presence-only statistics, background normalization, and probability calibration, differing only in that the nonlinearity is learned from data. Applied to 50-day environmental time series from ERA5 Land, MODIS, and Sentinel 3 with a 7-day gap for forecasting behavior.
AI.result: RNN Maxent outperforms standard Maxent: ROC AUC 0.862 (std 0.036) vs 0.792, and F1 0.671 (std 0.056) vs 0.590.
AI.conclusion: Learning nonlinear temporal relationships from data within the Maxent framework improves habitat suitability prediction for Desert Locust, demonstrating that neural sequence models can enhance presence-only SDM while preserving its statistical grounding.

title: Inferring Affective Consciousness in an Artificial Agent: A Case Study
summary: Creatures that display 'hedonic place preference behaviour' are thought by many scientists to experience feelings, on the assumption that their attraction to pleasure-producing substances which lack nutritional value (e.g. cocaine, morphine) cannot easily be attributed to unconscious instinctual behaviour. In this paper, we discuss how a simple artificial agent that instantiates attributes of an affective system engaging in felt uncertainty about its intrinsic needs in relation to environmental resources can similarly display hedonic place preference behaviour -- through an apparently subjective form of information processing -- while simultaneously being entirely deter-ministic. We outline some implications of this artificially engineered behaviour for our understanding of the physical basis of consciousness and the experience of free will.

AI.tldr: This paper demonstrates that a simple deterministic artificial agent with affective system attributes—engaging in felt uncertainty about intrinsic needs relative to environmental resources—can display hedonic place preference behavior (attraction to pleasure-producing substances lacking nutritional value), suggesting such behavior does not necessarily require consciousness or feelings.
AI.motivation: Scientists often interpret hedonic place preference behavior in creatures as evidence of subjective feelings, since attraction to nutritionally valueless pleasure substances (e.g., cocaine, morphine) seems hard to attribute to unconscious instinct. The authors challenge this assumption by exploring whether such behavior can emerge from purely deterministic mechanisms.
AI.method: The paper constructs a simple artificial agent that instantiates attributes of an affective system, specifically engaging in felt uncertainty about its intrinsic needs in relation to environmental resources. The agent's information processing is entirely deterministic yet apparently subjective in character, producing hedonic place preference behavior.
AI.result: The artificial, fully deterministic agent can indeed display hedonic place preference behavior through an apparently subjective form of information processing, demonstrating that such behavior need not rely on underlying consciousness or genuine feelings.
AI.conclusion: The findings have implications for understanding the physical basis of consciousness and the experience of free will—suggesting that behaviors often taken as evidence of subjective experience can emerge from deterministic processes, raising questions about how we infer consciousness and agency in biological and artificial systems.

title: Prospective Coding Improves Learning in Deep Continuous-Time Recurrent Networks
summary: Temporal integration gives continuous-time recurrent networks memory, but in deep stacks it also delays bottom-up signals and attenuates top-down errors. We develop Recursive Quadrature Filters (RQFs), biologically motivated complex-valued temporal filters that are a special case of diagonal state-space models (SSMs), and ask whether this failure mode can be addressed by making each layer's bottom-up input prospective. Starting from an energy model, we derive the RQF dynamics and show that each RQF is a band-pass filter whose learnable parameters control its tuning frequency and bandwidth. We then make each layer's bottom-up input prospective using a parameter-free two-tap update that leaves the recurrent transition and parallel scan unchanged. We extend this correction to general diagonal SSMs and show that it mitigates depth-dependent gradient attenuation when temporal gradients are truncated, i.e., spatial-only backpropagation. We evaluate the intervention in RQFs, S5, and ORGaNICs (a nonlinear gated RNN) trained using full backpropagation through time (BPTT) and spatial-only backpropagation. Under full BPTT, prospective variants match or outperform their non-prospective controls in every model and configuration. A non-residual width-32 six-layer RQF reaches 96.09% accuracy on raw-audio Speech Commands with 31.9k parameters; a width-64 six-layer RQF reaches 83.56% on the 16,384-step Path-X task. These results identify RQFs as a parameter-efficient recurrent substrate and prospective-input coding as an input-side correction for deep continuous-time recurrent networks.

AI.tldr: The paper develops Recursive Quadrature Filters (RQFs), biologically motivated complex-valued temporal filters (a special case of diagonal state-space models), and introduces a prospective-input correction that addresses depth-dependent gradient attenuation in deep continuous-time recurrent networks. RQFs achieve strong results on raw-audio Speech Commands and Path-X tasks with very few parameters.
AI.motivation: Deep stacks of continuous-time recurrent networks suffer from delayed bottom-up signals and attenuated top-down errors due to temporal integration, limiting their depth scalability despite the memory advantages temporal integration provides.
AI.method: Derive RQFs from an energy model as band-pass filters with learnable tuning frequency and bandwidth, make each layer's bottom-up input prospective using a parameter-free two-tap update (extended to general diagonal SSMs), and evaluate prospective variants in RQFs, S5, and ORGaNICs under both full BPTT and spatial-only backpropagation.
AI.result: Prospective variants match or outperform non-prospective controls across all models/configurations under full BPTT. A non-residual width-32 six-layer RQF achieves 96.09% on raw-audio Speech Commands (31.9k params); a width-64 six-layer RQF reaches 83.56% on the 16,384-step Path-X task.
AI.conclusion: RQFs are a parameter-efficient recurrent substrate, and prospective-input coding serves as an effective input-side correction for deep continuous-time recurrent networks, mitigating gradient attenuation during truncated temporal backpropagation.
